meta.title: Who really said "The truth will set you free, but first it will make you miserable"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — James A. Garfield never said it. The line is a modern twelve-step recovery adage, anonymous, first documented in 1978, decades after Garfield died.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The truth will set you free, but first it will make you miserable'?
meta.ogDescription: Not James A. Garfield. Quote Investigator traces this line to anonymous addiction-recovery literature, first documented 1978 — a century after Garfield's death.

answer.label: Not James A. Garfield — a modern recovery-movement adage
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence James A. Garfield ever said or wrote this. Garfield died in 1881, but the earliest documented appearance of the “make you miserable” wording is a 1978 newspaper report of a poster at an alcoholism-treatment facility, and Quote Investigator traces the saying to anonymous twelve-step recovery literature — never to Garfield.

source.excerpt: The truth will set you free, but first it will make you miserable.
trail: Quote Investigator finds the earliest “make you miserable” form in a 1978 Syracuse Herald-American report of a poster at an alcohol-treatment facility — anonymous, and with no link to Garfield.
The strongest early attributed use is Joe Klaas’s 1990 Twelve Steps to Happiness, where he calls the line (in its “piss you off” form) his “favorite motto” — again from recovery culture, per QI.
Goodreads explicitly logs this line as “often misattributed to President James Garfield,” underscoring that the presidential credit is a known error.
source.excerptNote: The wording circulates in many variants — “make you angry,” and Gloria Steinem’s well-known “first it will piss you off” — all sharing the same twelve-step-recovery pedigree rather than any presidential source.

author.name: James A. Garfield
author.heading: About James A. Garfield
author.bio: James Abram Garfield was a Union general, Ohio congressman, and the 20th U.S. President, serving only months in 1881 before he was shot in July and died that September. A lay preacher and classical scholar, he is genuinely quotable — which is exactly why feel-good aphorisms attach to his name. This one does not belong to him: he died nearly a century before the saying is first documented in 1970s addiction-recovery culture.

misattribution.heading: A misattribution magnet
misattribution.intro: This line is a classic “orphan aphorism” from twelve-step recovery culture that later got pinned onto famous names. None of the celebrity credits hold up.

items.why: Garfield died in 1881; the “make you miserable” wording is not documented until 1978. Quote Investigator’s full investigation never mentions Garfield, and it appears in none of his speeches or writings. Goodreads flags it as “often misattributed to President James Garfield.”
Steinem used the “first it will piss you off” form in speeches, but Quote Investigator shows she borrowed and reshaped an already-circulating recovery-movement saying rather than coining it.
Some quote sites (e.g. Goodreads) credit Gestalt writer Barry Stevens, but no primary source is cited and Quote Investigator traces the line to anonymous twelve-step literature instead.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: this is an anonymous twelve-step / recovery adage, first documented in 1978 — not a saying of President Garfield.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Garfield
lead: Garfield was a preacher and a scholar with a reputation for pithy moral sayings, so an aphorism about the painful cost of truth “sounds” presidential — and once one quote site prints the credit, others copy it. The chronology alone refutes it: he was assassinated in 1881, and the phrase does not surface until the late 1970s.

The saying’s real home is addiction-recovery culture, where truth-telling before liberation is a core theme. Its many variants — “make you miserable,” “make you angry,” “piss you off” — are the fingerprint of a folk adage passed mouth-to-mouth, not a fixed line from a documented speech.
context.pull: Garfield died in 1881. The quote isn’t written down until 1978.
